parsed.justification: Rationale A correctly identifies that the paper uses text descriptions to facilitate policy transfer and grounds reward/transition learning from text, but it overstates by saying the paper is not about learning reward functions from text at all — the paper does learn rewards from text descriptions, so the citation is not entirely unsupported. This slightly misapplies the rubric, which asks whether the context is compatible (score 1) rather than whether the paper's primary focus aligns exactly. Rationale B argues the paper learns reward functions directly from text and thus supports citation [27], which is reasonable since the paper does learn to map text descriptions to rewards. However, it somewhat oversimplifies — the paper's focus is on transfer learning via text-grounded dynamics, not purely 'learning reward functions directly from text.' The distinction is subtle but matters for the rubric. Both rationales partially capture the nuance but A is more careful in its evidence grounding, while B is slightly more generous in interpretation.
